steps: Step 1, Choose the greeting by time of day. Say "Good morning" before noon, "Good afternoon" after noon, and "Hello" or "Hi" any time. Model: "Good morning, Ms Rana." We use a short, friendly greeting first, before any other words.

Step 2, Give your name with "My name is" or the short form "I'm". Model: "Hello. My name is Tariq." Reason: the full form sounds clear and polite for a first meeting; the short form "I'm Tariq" is fine with friends.
Step 3, Ask and answer the name question as a pair. A: "What's your name?" B: "My name is Lina." Then turn it round: "And you?" Reason: "And you?" keeps the conversation going without a new question.
Step 4, Say your age with "I am" plus the number. Model: "I am eight." Ask: "How old are you?" Common error: "I have eight years." Correction: "I am eight." English uses the verb be for age.

Step 5, Spell your name by saying each letter slowly. Model: "My name is Lina. L, I, N, A." Say the vowels clearly: A is "ay", E is "ee", I is "eye". Pause after each letter so the listener can write it.
Step 6, Put it together as a mini-dialogue. A: "Hello! I'm Sam. What's your name?" B: "Hi, Sam. My name is Aisha. A, I, S, H, A." A: "How old are you?" B: "I am nine. And you?" A: "I am ten."

Step 7, Your turn. Write a four-line dialogue between you and a new classmate: greeting, name, age, spelling. Model answer: "Good afternoon. I'm Omar." / "Hi, Omar. My name is Jo. J, O." / "How old are you?" / "I am seven. And you?"

Step 1, Count from one to ten out loud: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Point to a finger for each number. Reason: matching the word to a real object makes the sound stick in memory.

Step 2, Continue to twenty and notice the pattern. Eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty. The teens end in "-teen". Stress falls on the end: thir-TEEN. Say each one twice.

Step 3, Name colours using a full sentence. Model: "The ball is red." "The leaf is green." Point to an object, then say its colour. Reason: a short sentence frame gives you a pattern you can reuse for every colour.
Step 4, Name shapes: circle, square, triangle, rectangle. Model: "It is a circle." Combine with colour: "It is a blue square." Word order matters: colour first, then shape.

Step 5, Fix a typical error. Wrong: "I have three red." Right: "I have three red pencils." After a number and colour we still need the thing we are counting. Also "thirteen" and "thirty" sound different: thir-TEEN, THIR-ty.

Step 6, Answer counting questions. A: "How many circles?" B: "Five circles." A: "What colour is the triangle?" B: "It is yellow." Reason: "How many" asks for a number; "What colour" asks for a colour word.
Step 7, Your turn. Draw two green triangles and four orange squares. Write two sentences about the picture. Model answer: "I have two green triangles." "I have four orange squares."

Step 1, List the family words in pairs: mother and father, sister and brother, grandmother and grandfather. Model: "This is my mother." "This is my brother." Use "This is" for one person and point to a photo.

Step 2, Introduce several people with "These are". Model: "These are my grandparents." Reason: "This" is for one person, "these" is for more than one. Error: "This are my sisters." Correction: "These are my sisters."

Step 3, Name rooms: kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, living room. Model: "This is the kitchen." Show a drawing of a house and touch each room as you say it. Reason: pointing links the new word to the place.
Step 4, Say where a person is with "is in". Model: "My mother is in the kitchen." "My brother is in the bedroom." Reason: "in" tells the place, and the verb "is" goes with one person.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "My father in the living room." Right: "My father is in the living room." Every sentence needs the verb "is" or "are". Say the correct sentence aloud three times.

Step 6, Make a mini-description. "This is my family. This is my mother. She is in the kitchen. This is my brother. He is in the bedroom." Reason: "she" and "he" replace names so we do not repeat them.
Step 7, Your turn. Write three sentences about your family and home. Model answer: "This is my sister. She is in the bathroom. My grandfather is in the living room."

Step 1, Name classroom objects with "It is a" before a consonant sound and "It is an" before a vowel sound. Model: "It is a pencil." "It is a book." "It is an eraser." Reason: "an" makes the vowel sound easier to say.
Step 2, Ask what something is. A: "What is this?" B: "It is a ruler." Point to the object as you ask. Reason: "this" means the thing is near you.

Step 3, Follow classroom instructions with action. "Stand up." "Sit down." "Open your book." "Close your bag." Do each action as soon as you hear it. Reason: acting out the words proves you understand.
Step 4, Add "please" to polite requests. Model: "Open your book, please." Answer a teacher with "Yes, Miss." Ask for help: "Can you help me, please?" Reason: "please" makes every request polite.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "This a pencil." Right: "This is a pencil." Do not drop "is". Another wrong sentence: "It is a umbrella." Right: "It is an umbrella", because umbrella starts with a vowel sound.

Step 6, Say a small classroom dialogue. Teacher: "Take out your pencil, please." Student: "Yes, Miss. Here is my pencil." Teacher: "Write your name." Student: "OK." Reason: short replies keep the lesson moving.

Step 7, Your turn. Write what the teacher says for four actions using the words stand, open, take out, write. Model answer: "Stand up, please." "Open your book." "Take out a pencil." "Write your name."

Step 1, Name foods and drinks you know: rice, bread, apple, banana, milk, water, juice. Say each with "I like". Model: "I like rice." Reason: "I like" plus a food word is the simplest pattern for opinions.
Step 2, Say what you do not like. Model: "I don't like milk." Pair the two: "I like bread, but I don't like milk." Reason: "don't" is the short form of "do not" and takes the plain food word.
Step 3, Ask a polite question about likes. A: "Do you like apples?" B: "Yes, I do." or "No, I don't." Reason: short answers repeat "do" and do not need the whole sentence.
Step 4, Ask for food politely. Model: "Can I have some water, please?" Answer: "Here you are." Reply: "Thank you." Reason: "Can I have" with "please" is the polite way to ask at a table.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Give me water." Right: "Can I have some water, please?" The first sounds like an order. Another error: "I no like fish." Right: "I don't like fish."
Step 6, Make a small dialogue. A: "Hello. Can I have some rice, please?" B: "Yes. Here you are." A: "Thank you. Can I have juice, please?" B: "Sorry, we have milk." A: "No, thank you."
Step 7, Your turn. Write what you like, what you do not like, and one polite request. Model answer: "I like bananas. I don't like fish. Can I have some juice, please?"

Step 1, Name animals: cat, dog, fish, bird, horse, cow. Model: "This is a dog." Point to a picture card for each one. Reason: matching a picture to a word is the fastest way to learn the first twenty animals.
Step 2, Name body parts: head, arm, leg, foot, eye, ear, nose, mouth. Touch each part as you say it. Model: "This is my nose." For two of a thing, say "These are my eyes."
Step 3, Say what an animal can do with "can". Model: "A bird can fly." "A fish can swim." "A horse can run." Reason: "can" stays the same for every animal and is followed by the plain verb.
Step 4, Say what an animal cannot do. Model: "A dog can't fly." Reason: "can't" is the short form of "cannot". Ask: "Can a cat swim?" Answer: "Yes, it can." or "No, it can't."
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "A fish can swims." Right: "A fish can swim." After "can" the verb never takes "s". Another error: "I have two ear." Right: "I have two ears."

Step 6, Describe an animal using body words and abilities. "This is a rabbit. It has two long ears and four legs. It can run. It can't swim." Reason: "has" is used for one animal, "have" for I and they.
Step 7, Your turn. Describe an animal you know in three sentences using a body part and can. Model answer: "This is a bird. It has two wings. It can fly, but it can't swim."
Step 1, Name clothes: shirt, dress, trousers, shoes, hat, coat. Model: "I wear a blue shirt." Use "wear" for what is on your body. Reason: "wear" shows the clothes are on you now.
Step 2, Say what someone else wears with "wears". Model: "She wears a red dress." "He wears black shoes." Reason: with he, she and it the verb takes "s". Say "I wear" but "he wears".
Step 3, Name weather words: sunny, rainy, windy, cold, hot, cloudy. Ask: "What's the weather like?" Answer: "It's sunny." Reason: "it" is the empty subject we use for weather.
Step 4, Link weather and clothes. Model: "It's cold, so I wear a coat." "It's rainy, so I wear boots." Reason: "so" joins the weather with the result of what we choose to wear.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "He wear a hat." Right: "He wears a hat." Another wrong sentence: "Is rainy today." Right: "It is rainy today." English sentences need a subject, even for weather.
Step 6, Make a short paragraph. "Today is Monday. It's windy and cold. I wear a coat and a hat. My sister wears a green scarf." Reason: each sentence has one idea, which is simple and clear.
Step 7, Your turn. Write three sentences about today's weather and what you wear. Model answer: "It's hot and sunny. I wear a white shirt. My brother wears shorts."

Step 1, Match a letter to its sound. The letter s says "sss", the letter m says "mmm", the letter a says "a" as in apple, the letter t says "t". Say the sound, not the letter name, when you read words.
Step 2, Blend sounds to read a word. For "mat": say "m", "a", "t" slowly, then run them together: "mat". Reason: blending each sound left to right is how we read new words.
Step 3, Read another group: "sat", "tap", "map". Change only the first sound: s-at, t-ap, m-ap. Reason: changing one letter shows how small sounds make new words.
Step 4, Fix an error. A child reads "cat" as "cut". Correction: look at the middle letter. The letter a says "a" and the letter u says "u". Slide a finger under each letter while you say the sound.
Step 5, Read a first sentence from known words: "A cat sat." Tap out each sound of "sat": s, a, t. Reason: a decodable sentence uses only letters you already know, so you can read it alone.

Step 6, Match words to pictures. Picture of a hat: the word "hat". Picture of a pin: the word "pin". Say the first sound, then the other sounds, then the whole word. Check that the picture and the word agree.
Step 7, Your turn. Read these words aloud sound by sound: "sit", "pan", "tin". Model answer: s-i-t, "sit"; p-a-n, "pan"; t-i-n, "tin". Then write one more word using m, a and p: "map".

Step 1, Listen for one thing at a time. Hear: "My name is Ben. I am nine. I like football." Listening task: what is his name? Answer: "Ben." Reason: choosing one detail makes a short talk easy to follow.
Step 2, Answer a simple question in a full sentence. Question: "How old is Ben?" Answer: "He is nine." Reason: repeating the words from the question helps you build a correct sentence.

Step 3, Use question words. "Who" asks for a person, "what" asks for a thing, "where" asks for a place. Question: "Where is Ben?" Answer: "He is at school." Match the question word to the kind of answer.
Step 4, Ask for help when you do not understand. Say: "Sorry, can you say that again, please?" or "Slowly, please." Reason: asking for repeats is a normal skill, and it is polite.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong answer to "What do you like?": "Yes." Right: "I like football." A "what" question needs a thing, not yes or no. Another error: "Where is Ben?" "Nine." The answer should be a place.
Step 6, Practise a short listen and answer. Teacher says: "I have a dog. Its name is Max. It is brown." Questions: "What is the dog's name?" "Max." "What colour is it?" "It is brown."
Step 7, Your turn. Listen to this and answer: "This is my friend Sara. She is ten. She likes books." What does Sara like? Model answer: "She likes books."
Step 1, Plan the talk in four short parts: greeting, name and age, family, likes. Reason: four small parts are easy to remember and give the talk a clear order.
Step 2, Write the model talk. "Hello. My name is Ali. I am eight. I have a mother, a father and one sister. I like football and rice." That is seven short sentences. Each has a subject and a verb.
Step 3, Practise saying each sentence aloud slowly. Stress the key words: "My name is ALI." "I am EIGHT." Reason: clear stress and a steady pace matter more than speed.
Step 4, Add one extra detail with "and". Model: "I have a cat and a dog." Reason: "and" joins two things in one sentence, so your talk sounds smoother.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "I am have a sister." Right: "I have a sister." We use "am" or "have", not both. Another error: "My name Ali." Right: "My name is Ali."

Step 6, Finish with a polite ending and a question. Model: "Thank you. Do you have any questions?" Answer a question like "How old are you?" with "I am eight." Reason: a closing line tells the listener the talk is over.
Step 7, Your turn. Write your own five-sentence talk. Model answer: "Hello. My name is Maya. I am nine. I have a brother and a cat. I like apples. Thank you."

Step 1, Write the day in time order using the present simple. Model: "I get up at six. I have breakfast at seven. I go to school at eight." Reason: the present simple describes habits, and each sentence names one action and one time.

Step 2, Add "s" for he, she and it. Model: "My brother gets up at seven. He brushes his teeth. She goes to school by bus." Reason: the third-person singular takes "-s", and "go" becomes "goes", "watch" becomes "watches".

Step 3, Use frequency words before the main verb. Model: "I usually walk to school. I never eat lunch at home." Reason: usually, often, sometimes and never sit before the verb but after "be": "I am always late."

Step 4, Make negatives and questions with do and does. Model: "I don't play games on Monday." "She doesn't eat meat." Question: "What time do you get up?" "Does he walk to school?" After does, the verb stays plain.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "She don't goes to school on Sunday." Right: "She doesn't go to school on Sunday." The helper does carries the "s", so the main verb returns to its base form.

Step 6, Write a short paragraph. "On school days I get up at six. I wash and have breakfast. Then I go to school by bus. After school I do my homework. I go to bed at nine." Reason: time words like then and after link events.

Step 7, Your turn. Write four sentences about a friend's day using he or she and one frequency word. Model answer: "My friend gets up at six. She usually walks to school. She doesn't watch TV on weekdays. She goes to bed at ten."

Step 1, Learn place words: bank, post office, library, market, hospital, park, bus station. Model: "The library is next to the park." Reason: "next to", "opposite", "between" and "behind" place one building by another.
Step 2, Ask for directions politely. Model: "Excuse me, where is the post office?" or "How do I get to the bank?" Reason: "Excuse me" gets attention, and the question is clear and short.

Step 3, Give directions with imperatives. Model: "Go straight on. Turn left at the traffic lights. Then turn right. The bank is on your left." Reason: verbs at the start of a sentence give direct, clear instructions.
Step 4, Use distance and landmark words. Model: "Walk for two minutes. It's opposite the market." Reason: a landmark, such as the market, helps the listener check they are going the right way.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Turn to left and go straight." Right: "Turn left and go straight." We say "turn left" without "to". Another error: "It is in front the bank." Right: "It is in front of the bank."
Step 6, Practise a full dialogue. A: "Excuse me, where is the library?" B: "Go straight on. Turn right at the park. It's next to the school." A: "Thank you very much." B: "You're welcome."

Step 7, Your turn. You are at the bus station. Give directions to the hospital: straight, then left at the bank, opposite the park. Model answer: "Go straight on. Turn left at the bank. The hospital is opposite the park."

Step 1, Say what you like with verb plus -ing or a noun. Model: "I like swimming." "I love football." "I don't like running." Reason: after like, love and hate we often use the -ing form for activities.
Step 2, Say what you can do with can plus the base verb. Model: "I can play chess." "She can swim very well." Reason: "can" never changes and the next verb has no "s" or "-ing".
Step 3, Ask and answer about hobbies. A: "What do you do in your free time?" B: "I play cricket and I read stories." A: "Can you play the guitar?" B: "No, I can't, but I can sing."
Step 4, Link with and, but and because. Model: "I like tennis, but I can't play it well." "I like painting because it's relaxing." Reason: "but" shows contrast and "because" gives the reason.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "She can swims fast." Right: "She can swim fast." Another wrong: "I like play football." Right: "I like playing football" or "I like to play football."
Step 6, Write a short paragraph. "My name is Ravi. I like cycling and swimming. I play cricket on Saturday. I can't play tennis, but I can play table tennis. I like sport because it's fun."

Step 7, Your turn. Write four sentences about your own hobbies including one can and one but. Model answer: "I like drawing. I play football on Friday. I can swim, but I can't dive. I like music because it is relaxing."
Step 1, Ask the price with "How much". Model: "How much is this shirt?" for one item and "How much are these shoes?" for plural items. Reason: use is for singular and are for plural.
Step 2, Say the answer with the price. Model: "It's twelve dollars." "They are twenty-five dollars." Read prices as words: 4.50 is "four dollars fifty". Reason: say the big unit, then the small one.
Step 3, Ask for what you want politely. Model: "I'd like a notebook, please." "Can I have two pens?" Reason: "I'd like" is the polite short form of "I would like".

Step 4, Pay and check change. Customer: "Here is ten dollars." Seller: "Thank you. Here's your change, three dollars." Customer: "Thank you." Reason: "change" is the money returned, and it is never plural.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "How much cost this bag?" Right: "How much is this bag?" or "How much does this bag cost?" Another error: "I want a bread." Right: "I'd like some bread."
Step 6, Practise the full shopping dialogue. A: "Hello, I'd like an orange juice." B: "That's two dollars." A: "How much are those apples?" B: "They're three dollars a kilo." A: "I'll take one kilo."

Step 7, Your turn. Write a four-line dialogue buying a pen that costs one dollar fifty with a five-dollar note. Model answer: "How much is this pen?" "It's one dollar fifty." "Here is five dollars." "Thank you. Here's your change."
Step 1, Use the past simple for finished actions with a time word like yesterday. Model: "Yesterday I played football." Regular verbs add "-ed": play, played; walk, walked; clean, cleaned.

Step 2, Learn irregular verbs. Go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, have becomes had. Model: "We went to the market and saw a monkey." Reason: these common verbs change form and must be remembered.
Step 3, Make negatives and questions with did. Model: "I didn't watch TV." "Did you finish your homework?" Answer: "Yes, I did." Reason: after did and didn't the verb returns to the base form.

Step 4, Order a story with sequence words. "First I got up late. Then I ate breakfast. After that I went to school. Finally I came home." Reason: first, then, after that and finally show the order of events.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Yesterday I go to the park." Right: "Yesterday I went to the park." Another error: "She didn't went." Right: "She didn't go." The past mark is on did only.
Step 6, Write a short story. "Yesterday was Sunday. I got up at eight and ate rice. Then I visited my grandmother. We cooked dinner together. I went to bed early because I was tired."

Step 7, Your turn. Write four sentences about what you did yesterday using two irregular verbs. Model answer: "Yesterday I went to school. I saw my friend. After lunch I played cricket. In the evening I did my homework."
Step 1, Describe people with adjectives after "be": tall, short, kind, funny, quiet. Model: "My uncle is tall and funny." Put the adjective before a noun too: "He is a kind man."
Step 2, Describe things with colour, size and shape in that order of importance for beginners. Model: "I have a small round red ball." Reason: opinion and size words generally come before colour.

Step 3, Make short comparatives with "-er than". Model: "Anil is taller than Bina." "This bag is lighter than that bag." Reason: for one-syllable adjectives add "-er" and use "than" before the second thing.

Step 4, Make longer comparatives with "more". Model: "The film is more interesting than the book." "A car is more expensive than a bicycle." Reason: adjectives of two or more syllables use "more" instead of "-er".

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "She is more tall than me." Right: "She is taller than me." Another: "This is more good." Right: "This is better." Irregular: good, better; bad, worse. For "big", double the g: bigger.
Step 6, Compare two things in a paragraph. "My dog is bigger than my cat. The cat is quieter than the dog. The dog is friendlier, but the cat is cleaner."

Step 7, Your turn. Compare two animals using three sentences with one -er and one more. Model answer: "A horse is faster than a cow. A cow is heavier than a goat. A horse is more beautiful than a cow, in my opinion."
Step 1, Say how you feel using "I feel" or "I am" plus an adjective: happy, sad, tired, angry, nervous. Model: "I feel tired today." "I am happy because my friend is here."
Step 2, Say what is wrong with "have a" or "my ... hurts". Model: "I have a headache." "I have a sore throat." "My stomach hurts." Reason: English uses "have a" for common ailments.

Step 3, Talk to a doctor. Doctor: "What's the matter?" Patient: "I have a fever and a cough." Doctor: "How long have you felt like this?" Patient: "Since yesterday." Reason: "since" names the start time.
Step 4, Give advice with should. Model: "You should rest." "You should drink water." "You shouldn't go to school today." Reason: "should" is followed by the base verb and is used for advice.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "I am headache." Right: "I have a headache." Another wrong: "You should to rest." Right: "You should rest." There is no "to" after should.
Step 6, Practise a full dialogue. A: "You look sick. What's the matter?" B: "I have a bad cold." A: "You should go home and rest." B: "Yes, I think so. Thank you."
Step 7, Your turn. Write three lines saying how you feel, what is wrong, and one piece of advice. Model answer: "I feel terrible. I have a sore throat. You should drink warm water and rest."

Step 1, Preview the topic before the audio. If the audio is about a bus timetable, expect times, places and numbers. Reason: knowing what to expect helps you notice the key details instead of every word.

Step 2, Take notes with short words and symbols. Hear: "The bus to the lake leaves at half past eight from stop five." Note: "bus - lake - 8.30 - stop 5." Reason: notes keep only the facts and drop the extra words.
Step 3, Listen for numbers carefully. Fifteen and fifty sound alike: fif-TEEN has the stress at the end, and FIF-ty at the start. Model note: "15 min" or "50 min". Replay the line to check.

Step 4, Write answers from notes in full sentences. Notes: "bus - lake - 8.30 - stop 5." Answer: "The bus to the lake leaves at eight thirty from stop five." Reason: a sentence made from notes sounds complete and accurate.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong note: "bus 8.13" when the speaker said "eight-thirty". Hint: "-teen" sounds end strongly, but "thirty" starts strongly. Check with another detail, such as "half past".
Step 6, Practise with a short script. Audio: "The market opens at nine on Tuesday and Friday. Entry is free. It's near the old bridge." Notes: "market - 9 - Tue, Fri - free - old bridge."

Step 7, Your turn. Audio: "The swimming class is on Wednesday at four. Bring a towel. The teacher is Mr Khan." Take notes and write two answers. Model answer: notes "swim - Wed - 4 - towel - Mr Khan"; "The class is on Wednesday at four."
Step 1, Pick a project topic you can describe: "My favourite place". Plan three parts: introduction, three details, ending. Reason: a clear plan keeps your talk short and easy to follow.
Step 2, Write the introduction. "Hello, everyone. My project is about my favourite place, the lake near my village. I'm going to tell you where it is, what I do there, and why I like it."

Step 3, Write the details with present simple and past simple. "It is five minutes from my house. On Sundays I swim and fish. Last summer I saw a white bird there." Reason: present simple gives habits and past simple gives a memory.
Step 4, Add reasons with because and a comparison. "I like it because it is quiet. It is cleaner than the river." Reason: reasons and comparisons make the talk more interesting than simple facts.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "I am going to tell you about my place is nice." Right: "I'm going to tell you about my place. It is nice." Keep each sentence to one main verb.

Step 6, Finish and invite questions. "Thank you for listening. Does anyone have a question?" Answer: "Yes, I go there on foot, about ten minutes." Reason: a closing line signals the end and invites response.

Step 7, Your turn. Write a four-sentence introduction and ending for a project on your favourite food. Model answer: "Hello, everyone. My project is about rice. I eat it every day because it is cheap and tasty. Thank you. Any questions?"
Step 1, Choose going to for plans already decided. Model: "I'm going to visit my cousin next week." Form: be plus going to plus the base verb. Reason: the plan was made before the moment of speaking.

Step 2, Choose will for sudden decisions and predictions. Model: "It's cold. I'll close the window." "I think it will rain tomorrow." Reason: the decision happens now, and a prediction is an opinion about the future.
Step 3, Make negatives and questions. Model: "I'm not going to work this weekend." "Are you going to study tonight?" "She won't come." Reason: won't is will not, and the main verb stays plain.

Step 4, Compare in one sentence. "I'm going to study medicine; I think I'll enjoy it." Reason: the plan uses going to, the guess about enjoying uses will. Time words: tomorrow, next year, in two weeks, soon.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Tomorrow I will to go to the market." Right: "Tomorrow I will go to the market." Another wrong: "I going to eat." Right: "I'm going to eat." Never omit the form of be.
Step 6, Ask about plans. A: "What are you going to do this summer?" B: "I'm going to visit my grandparents, and I'll help on the farm." A: "That sounds great. I think you'll enjoy it."

Step 7, Your turn. Write three sentences: a plan, a prediction and a sudden decision. Model answer: "I'm going to start a sports club. I think it will be popular. Oh, the phone is ringing; I'll answer it."

Step 1, Describe a trip in the past simple with details. Model: "Last July we travelled to the coast by train. The journey took four hours. We stayed in a small hotel near the beach." Reason: the past simple tells the story.
Step 2, Add feeling and description. "The sea was clear and warm. The food was delicious, but the town was crowded." Reason: adjectives make a trip description specific, and "but" shows contrast.

Step 3, Book a ticket politely. Customer: "I'd like two return tickets to Kandy, please." Clerk: "When are you travelling?" Customer: "Next Saturday, in the morning." Reason: "return" means there and back; "single" means one way.
Step 4, Ask about times and prices. "What time does the train leave?" "How long does the journey take?" "Is there a seat by the window?" Reason: present simple questions are used for timetables.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "I want two ticket to Kandy." Right: "I'd like two tickets to Kandy." Another error: "We have gone to the coast last July." Right: "We went to the coast last July."
Step 6, Write a short postcard. "Dear Maya, We are having a great time at the coast. The weather is sunny, and we swim every day. Tomorrow we are going to visit a fort. See you soon, Imran."

Step 7, Your turn. Write a three-line dialogue booking one single bus ticket to the capital for tomorrow. Model answer: "I'd like a single ticket to the capital, please." "For which day?" "Tomorrow morning, please."

Step 1, State your opinion with a fixed phrase. Model: "In my opinion, students should wear uniform." Alternatives: "I think that", "I believe that", "As far as I'm concerned". Reason: a phrase shows that you are giving a view, not a fact.
Step 2, Give a reason with because. "I think students should wear uniform because it makes everyone equal." Reason: because answers the question why, and the reason follows it directly.
Step 3, Give a result with so. "Uniforms are cheap, so families save money." Reason: "so" shows the result, while "because" shows the cause. Compare: "Families save money because uniforms are cheap."
Step 4, Agree and disagree politely. "I agree with you." "I see your point, but I think it is too strict." Reason: starting with "I see your point" keeps the tone respectful.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Because it is cheap, so I like it." Right: "I like it because it is cheap" or "It is cheap, so I like it." Never use both because and so in one clause.
Step 6, Build a mini-paragraph. "I think homework is useful because it helps us remember. It also builds a habit, so we study better. However, too much homework is tiring."

Step 7, Your turn. Give your opinion on school lunch with one because and one so. Model answer: "I think school should serve hot lunch because students learn better when they are not hungry. It is healthy, so parents are happy too."
Step 1, Plan an email with four parts: greeting, reason for writing, details, closing. Reason: a plan lets the reader find the key information quickly.

Step 2, Write a friendly email. "Hi Nadia, Thanks for your message. I'm writing to ask about Saturday. Are you free at three? Let me know. Best wishes, Hamid." Use contractions for friends, and "Dear" for a teacher.

Step 3, Write a formal email with polite phrases. "Dear Mr Silva, I am writing to ask whether I can borrow a book from the library. I would be grateful for your reply. Yours sincerely, Hamid." Reason: formal emails avoid contractions.

Step 4, Write a short note. "Mum, I've gone to Ravi's house to study. I'll be back at six. Don't wait for dinner. Love, Hamid." Reason: a note is short, gives the key facts, and uses no long greeting.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Dear Sir, i want the book now." Right: "Dear Sir, I would like to borrow the book, please." Capital I, polite request, and a complete sentence make the email correct.
Step 6, Correct the closing. For a name you know: "Best wishes" or "Kind regards". For a teacher: "Yours sincerely" if you know the name. Reason: closings show how formal the email is.

Step 7, Your turn. Write a three-sentence email to a friend inviting him to your birthday on Sunday at five. Model answer: "Hi Sam, I'm having a birthday party on Sunday at five. Can you come? Please tell me by Friday. Best wishes, Hamid."

Step 1, Listen for the main idea first. Teacher: "Today we'll learn how plants make food. Leaves use sunlight, water and air." Main idea: how plants make food. Reason: you find the topic before the details.
Step 2, Spot signpost words. "First", "next", "so", "for example" and "in conclusion" tell you how ideas link. Model note: "First: roots take in water." Reason: signposts help you order the notes.
Step 3, Take brief notes. Teacher: "Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and sunlight gives them energy." Note: "leaves - CO2 + light = energy." Reason: notes need keywords only.

Step 4, Ask a clarifying question politely. "Sorry, could you explain what photosynthesis means?" or "Could you repeat the second point, please?" Reason: you ask about words you missed, not the whole lesson.
Step 5, Fix an error. A student writes: "Plants make light." The teacher said: "Plants use light to make food." Check the verb. Corrected note: "plants use light to make food."

Step 6, Summarise in two sentences. "The teacher explained how plants make food. They use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, and they produce sugar and oxygen." Reason: a summary has the main idea plus the key detail.

Step 7, Your turn. Teacher says: "The water cycle has three steps. Water evaporates, it condenses into clouds, and it falls as rain." Write notes and one summary sentence. Model answer: "water cycle: evaporate - condense - rain." "Water rises, makes clouds, and falls as rain."
Step 1, Plan a talk with a hook, three points and a close. Topic: "A day without phones". Hook: "Imagine one whole day without your phone." Reason: a hook gains attention.

Step 2, Write each point with a reason. "First, we would talk more with our family. Second, we would sleep better, because there's no screen at night. Finally, we would read more." Reason: first, second and finally make the structure obvious.
Step 3, Add a counter-view. "Some people say they need phones for safety. That's true, but we can use them only for calls." Reason: showing you know another view makes your opinion stronger.

Step 4, Practise answering questions. Q: "Would you really do it?" A: "Yes, I think I would, but only for one day." Q: "Why?" A: "Because I want to see if I can." Reason: answers start with a direct response, then a reason.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "If I will have no phone, I sleep more." Right: "If I had no phone, I would sleep more." Or simple: "If I have no phone, I'll sleep more." Match the tenses in both clauses.

Step 6, Close the talk clearly. "To sum up, a day without phones would improve my family time, my sleep and my reading. Thank you. I'm happy to answer questions." Reason: "to sum up" signals the ending.

Step 7, Your turn. Write the hook and the close for a talk on "Why I like my town". Model answer: "Hook: What makes a town feel like home?" "Close: To sum up, my town is friendly, safe and green. Thank you. Any questions?"

Step 1, Read the text once for the main idea, then mark key words. Text: "Urban gardens grow food in small city spaces. They reduce transport costs and give neighbours a shared project." Main idea: city gardens benefit food supply and community.

Step 2, Take notes with a heading and abbreviations. Model: "Urban gardens: = food in small city spaces; benefits: 1. cheaper transport, 2. community project." Reason: arrows, numbers and keywords replace full sentences and save time.

Step 3, Separate main points from examples. Main point: gardens reduce costs. Example: "tomatoes grown on a roof need no lorry." Reason: a summary keeps the main points and usually drops the examples.
Step 4, Paraphrase instead of copying. Original: "give neighbours a shared project." Paraphrase: "bring local people together." Reason: new wording shows understanding and avoids copying the source.

Step 5, Write the summary in about forty words. "Urban gardens produce food in small city areas. They lower transport costs and encourage neighbours to work together. As a result, they improve both local food supply and community life."
Step 6, Fix an error. Weak: "I think urban gardens are great and my uncle has one." Better: remove personal opinion and detail. A summary is neutral, shorter than the original, and in your own words.

Step 7, Your turn. Text: "Libraries now offer digital books, which readers borrow online. This saves travel time and lets people read without paying." Write notes and a one-sentence summary. Model answer: "Libraries lend digital books online, saving readers time and money."

Step 1, Divide the time before you start. For a 60-minute paper with three sections, give reading 20 minutes, writing 30 minutes, checking 10 minutes. Reason: a fixed plan stops you from spending too long on one task.

Step 2, Read the instruction line carefully. Question: "Write 100-120 words about a day you remember." Underline: "100-120 words", "a day you remember". Reason: word limits and topic words are easily missed.

Step 3, Notice command words. "Describe" means give details, "explain" means give reasons, "compare" means show similarity and difference. Model: for "Explain why", start "This happened because..." Reason: the command word decides the answer type.

Step 4, Answer a multiple-choice item by checking each option. Question: "The writer feels worried." Options: A "calm", B "nervous", C "proud". Text says "her hands shook". Answer: B. Reason: pick the option that matches evidence in the text.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: writing 200 words when asked for 100-120 and having no time to check. Right: write a short plan of three bullets, then write about 110 words and keep two minutes for checking.

Step 6, Use a checking list at the end. "Did I answer every part? Are my verbs in the right tense? Capital letters and full stops? Spelling of difficult words?" Reason: a routine catches small errors fast.

Step 7, Your turn. A 40-minute reading test has 4 passages. Plan your time. Model answer: about 8 minutes reading and answering each passage, which leaves 8 minutes to check, so skip a hard question and return to it later.

Step 1, Check your sentence control with a short paragraph. Model: "Although I was nervous, I spoke clearly. My teacher said my presentation was well organised." Reason: a joined sentence with although shows you can combine ideas accurately.

Step 2, Review verb tenses in one passage. "Yesterday I went to the library. I am going to borrow two books. I have read one already." Reason: past simple, going to and present perfect show three time frames used correctly.

Step 3, Check word choice and connectors. Weak: "It was good. And then it was good again." Better: "The first lesson was useful; moreover, the second was interesting." Connectors: however, therefore, in addition.

Step 4, Write a short opinion paragraph. "I believe students should learn to cook because it builds independence. Furthermore, it encourages healthy eating. Therefore, schools should include cooking classes." Reason: claim, reason, extension and conclusion.

Step 5, Fix typical errors. Wrong: "Each of the students have a book." Right: "Each of the students has a book." Wrong: "I am agree." Right: "I agree." Check subject-verb agreement and do not use be before agree.

Step 6, Speak your readiness aloud. Prompt: "What did you enjoy about your course?" Answer: "I enjoyed the group projects because they helped me practise speaking, and I became more confident." Reason: give an answer plus a reason.

Step 7, Your turn. Write three sentences about your progress using one connector and two tenses. Model answer: "I have improved my speaking. Last term I was shy; however, now I join discussions. Next year I am going to write longer essays."

Step 1, Say the first sounds with a picture. s for sun, a for ant, t for tap, p for pin, i for ink, n for net. Say the sound, not the letter name: "sss", not "ess". Reason: sounds, not names, build words.
Step 2, Blend three sounds into a word. s-a-t: touch each letter, say each sound, then slide them together: "sat". Reason: touching and sliding keeps the child going left to right.
Step 3, Swap one sound to make a new word. sat, pat, pan, pin. Only one sound changes each time. Reason: noticing which letter changed shows how each sound matters.
Step 4, Fix an error. The child reads "pin" as "pan". Correction: look at the middle letter. The letter i says "i" as in ink. Point to it and blend again: p-i-n, "pin".

Step 5, Say the sounds in order: a, b, c, d, e, f... as sounds: "a" as in apple, "b" as in ball, "c" as in cat. Match each letter card to a picture card. Reason: matching practises both sound and shape.

Step 6, Write and say a sentence with blended words: "A cat sat on a mat." Point to each word as you read. Words to blend: c-a-t, s-a-t, m-a-t. Reason: reading a real sentence gives the sounds a purpose.
Step 7, Your turn. Blend these words: "tip", "nap", "tin". Model answer: t-i-p "tip"; n-a-p "nap"; t-i-n "tin". Now make a new word by changing the first sound of "tin" to "p": "pin".

Step 1, Read tricky words you cannot sound out by sight. Words like "the", "is", "was", "you", "said". Say them, cover them, and say them again. Reason: these common words are used in nearly every sentence.
Step 2, Decode a regular word. Word: "frog". Say each sound: f-r-o-g. Blend the first two: "fr", add "o", add "g": "frog". Reason: blends like fr, st and cl are read as two sounds quickly together.
Step 3, Read a short sentence with both types. "The frog is on a log." Sight words: "the", "is", "on", "a". Decodable words: "frog", "log". Point and read smoothly.

Step 4, Fix an error. The child reads "was" as "wass". Correction: "was" is a sight word and says "woz". Practise by covering and reading it five times quickly. Reason: not every word follows the sound rule.
Step 5, Check meaning after reading. Sentence: "The dog ran to the pond." Question: "Where did the dog run?" Answer: "To the pond." Reason: reading is understanding, not only sounding out.

Step 6, Read a two-sentence story. "A big ant sat on a leaf. The ant said, 'I am hot.'" Notice speech marks around what the ant says. Point to the full stop at the end of each sentence and take a short pause.
Step 7, Your turn. Read this and answer: "The cat is on the bed. It is big." What is on the bed? Model answer: "The cat is on the bed." It is big.

Step 1, Form letters from the right starting point. The letter c starts at the top right, curves left round and stops. The letter a starts the same way and then draws a straight line down. Say the path aloud as you write.
Step 2, Keep letters the right height. Tall letters (b, d, h, l) reach the top line; short letters (a, c, e, o) sit in the middle. Write "bad" and check: b and d are tall, a is short.
Step 3, Write your first name with one capital letter. Model: "Nora". The capital N is tall, the other letters are small. Reason: names always start with a capital letter.

Step 4, Fix an error. The child writes "nora" or "NORA". Correction: "Nora", capital first, lowercase after. Another error: letter b facing backwards. Fix: draw the straight line first, then the circle to its right ("bat and ball").
Step 5, Leave spaces between words. Write "my cat" with a finger-width gap between the words. Reason: gaps make the words easy to read, and a finger space gives the correct size.
Step 6, Write labels for pictures. A picture of a hat: label "hat". A picture of a dog: label "dog". Say the sounds as you write: h-a-t. Reason: saying the sounds helps you spell the word.
Step 7, Your turn. Write your name and a label for a drawing of a sun. Model answer: "Nora" at the top, and under the sun picture write "sun".

Step 1, Sort naming words into four groups: people, animals, places, things. People: teacher, mother. Animals: cat, goat. Places: school, shop. Things: book, ball. Reason: a noun names someone or something.
Step 2, Say a sentence for each group. "The teacher is kind." "The cat is soft." "The school is big." "The ball is red." Reason: the noun is the main word in each sentence.
Step 3, Use "a" or "an" before a noun. "a cat", "a school", "an egg", "an animal". Reason: "an" goes before the vowel sounds a, e, i, o, u, and "a" goes before other sounds.
Step 4, Make more than one with -s. One dog, two dogs. One book, three books. Reason: adding s changes a naming word from one to many. Say each pair aloud and hear the final s.

Step 5, Fix an error. The child puts "run" in the animal group. Correction: "run" is something we do; it is not a thing or animal. Put "dog" there. Ask: "Can I see it, touch it, or name it as a place or person?"
Step 6, Sort a mixed list. Words: mum, park, lion, pen, Sara, farm. People: mum, Sara. Places: park, farm. Animals: lion. Things: pen. Notice "Sara" begins with a capital letter because it is a name.
Step 7, Your turn. Sort: boy, tree, bus, bird, kitchen. Model answer: people: boy. Animals: bird. Places: kitchen. Things: tree, bus. Make a sentence: "The bird is in the tree."
Step 1, Act out an action word. Say "jump" and jump. Say "clap" and clap. List them: run, hop, sit, eat, write. Reason: an action word tells what someone does.
Step 2, Put the action word in a sentence. "The boy runs." "The girl jumps." "I sit on a mat." Reason: every sentence needs a naming word and an action word.
Step 3, Use the right ending with one person. "The dog runs." "The cat sleeps." For more than one: "The dogs run." "I run." Reason: the verb takes -s after he, she, it or one thing.
Step 4, Ask a question about an action. "What does the boy do?" "He kicks the ball." Reason: "do" asks about an action, and the answer repeats the action word.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "The boy run." Right: "The boy runs." Another error: "The cat jump high." Right: "The cat jumps high." Listen to the s sound at the end when one thing is doing the action.
Step 6, Make a sentence from a word bank. Words: "The bird" and "flies", "sings", "eats". Model: "The bird flies." "The bird sings." "The bird eats." Check each has a capital letter and a full stop.
Step 7, Your turn. Write two sentences using the action words swim and read. Model answer: "The fish swims." "I read a book." Check: capital letter, action word, full stop.
Step 1, Retell a short story in three parts. Story: "A hen found a seed. She planted it. It grew into a big tree." Beginning: the hen finds a seed. Middle: she plants it. End: a tree grows.
Step 2, Use story words. "First, the hen found a seed. Next, she planted it. At the end, a tree grew." Reason: first, next and at the end show the order of events.
Step 3, Join in with a rhyme. "Hen, ten" and "tree, three" rhyme because they share the end sound. Say: "One hen, two hens, three hens, ten." Clap the beat as you say it.
Step 4, Find rhyming words. Pairs: cat and hat, bug and rug, star and car. Reason: the end sounds match, even if the spelling differs a little.
Step 5, Fix an error. The child tells the end before the middle. Correction: ask "What happened first? What happened next? How did it end?" Reason: events must follow the order of the story.

Step 6, Draw and say three pictures. Picture 1: a boy with a kite. Picture 2: the kite flies high. Picture 3: the kite gets stuck in a tree. Retell: "The boy has a kite. It flies high. It gets stuck."
Step 7, Your turn. Retell this: "A cat sat on a wall. It saw a bird. The bird flew away." Model answer: "First, the cat sat on a wall. Next, it saw a bird. At the end, the bird flew away."
Step 1, Take turns when talking. Rule: one person speaks, the others listen. Model: "It is your turn, Sam." "Thank you. I like red." Reason: waiting for your turn shows respect.
Step 2, Listen to a two-step instruction. Teacher: "Pick up your pencil and write your name." Do two actions in order: first pick up, then write. Reason: listening carefully means doing every step.

Step 3, Answer in a full sentence. Question: "What is your favourite food?" Answer: "My favourite food is rice." Not just "Rice." Reason: a full sentence has a naming word and an action or being word.
Step 4, Speak so people can hear. Use a loud, clear voice and look at the listener. Model: "Good morning. My name is Ana." Reason: a clear voice and eye contact make you easier to understand.
Step 5, Fix an error. Question: "Where do you live?" Child: "Near." Better: "I live near the market." Another error: speaking while someone else is talking. Correction: wait, then say "Excuse me."
Step 6, Ask a question back. "I like cats. Do you like cats?" Answer: "Yes, I do." Reason: a question keeps a conversation going.
Step 7, Your turn. Answer in a full sentence: "What do you do after school?" Model answer: "After school I play with my friends." Then ask a question: "What do you do after school?"

Step 1, Learn vowel pairs as sound teams. ai and ay say "ay": rain, tray. ee and ea say "ee": feet, leaf. oa says "oh": boat. Sort words by the sound, then check the spelling. Reason: a pair shares one sound.
Step 2, Choose ai or ay by position. Use "ai" in the middle of a word (rain, paint) and "ay" at the end (play, day). Model: "We play in the rain." Reason: English words rarely end in "ai".
Step 3, Read and spell blends. Blends: st, bl, cr, tr, sp. Word: "stamp" = s-t-a-m-p. Say the first two sounds quickly, then the vowel, then the end. Spell "crab": c-r-a-b.
Step 4, Fix an error. A child spells "boat" as "bote" or "rain" as "rane". Correction: bo-a-t uses the vowel pair oa, and r-ai-n uses ai. Say the word, tap the sounds, and write the pair together.
Step 5, Spell with the "say, tap, write" method. Word: "green". Say it, tap g-r-ee-n (four sounds), and write it. Check: the ee pair is two letters for one sound. Cover and write it again.
Step 6, Write a sentence using three pattern words. "The goat sat in the rain by the green tree." Pattern words: goat (oa), rain (ai), green (ee). Check spelling of each pair.
Step 7, Your turn. Spell these as you hear them: tray, leaf, coat. Model answer: t-r-ay, l-ea-f, c-oa-t. Then write one sentence: "I put my coat on the tray."

Step 1, Read for sense. Passage: "Tom has a red kite. He flies it in the park on Sunday. His sister Mia helps him." Read aloud smoothly, pausing at each full stop. Reason: stops give breath and meaning.
Step 2, Answer a who question. "Who has a kite?" Answer: "Tom has a kite." Find the name in the text and give a complete sentence. Reason: who asks about a person.
Step 3, Answer a what and where question. "What does Tom fly?" "He flies a red kite." "Where does he fly it?" "In the park." Reason: what asks about a thing; where asks for a place.
Step 4, Use the text to check. Question: "When does Tom fly the kite?" Answer: "On Sunday." Point to the words in the passage. Reason: the answer must come from the text, not from a guess.
Step 5, Fix an error. Question: "Who helps Tom?" Wrong answer: "The park." Right: "His sister Mia helps him." A who question needs a person. Read the question word first before you answer.
Step 6, Read with expression. A question ends with a rising voice: "Can you fly the kite?" An exclamation is stronger: "It is high!" Reason: punctuation tells you how to read.
Step 7, Your turn. Passage: "Ben has a cat. It sleeps on a mat by the door." Answer: Who has a cat? Where does it sleep? Model answer: "Ben has a cat." "It sleeps on a mat by the door."

Step 1, Tell common from proper nouns. Common nouns name any one of a kind: girl, city, river. Proper nouns name a particular one: Sara, Lahore, Nile. Proper nouns begin with capital letters. Reason: they are special names.
Step 2, Sort a list. Words: boy, Omar, school, Green Hill School, dog, Rex. Common: boy, school, dog. Proper: Omar, Green Hill School, Rex. Reason: "dog" is any dog, "Rex" is one dog.
Step 3, Fix capital letters in a sentence. Wrong: "my friend aisha lives in karachi." Right: "My friend Aisha lives in Karachi." Capitals: the first word, the name Aisha, and the city Karachi.
Step 4, Capitalise days and months. Model: "On Monday in March we visit Cairo." Days, months and place names are proper nouns. But seasons are common: "We visit in spring."
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "We went to the Park with Our Dog." Right: "We went to the park with our dog." Only proper names get capitals. If the dog was named Max: "with our dog Max."
Step 6, Write a sentence with both. "The teacher, Mr Khan, gave a book to the girl." Common: teacher, book, girl. Proper: Mr Khan. Reason: the title and name together are one proper noun.
Step 7, Your turn. Rewrite with correct capitals: "last tuesday zara and her dog bruno went to the river." Model answer: "Last Tuesday Zara and her dog Bruno went to the river."
Step 1, Start with a plain sentence. "The dog barked." Add an adjective: "The big dog barked." Add a stronger verb: "The big dog howled." Reason: adjectives describe nouns and verbs show the action.
Step 2, Choose strong verbs. Plain: "walk". Stronger: "stroll", "stride", "creep", depending on the meaning. Model: "The cat crept across the floor." Reason: a precise verb paints a clearer picture.

Step 3, Choose adjectives that tell more than "nice". Instead of "a nice day", write "a bright, warm day". Use a comma between two adjectives of equal weight. Reason: precise adjectives give sensory details.
Step 4, Add where and when. "Yesterday the big dog howled loudly at the gate." Added: when (yesterday), how (loudly), where (at the gate). Reason: each detail answers a question the reader may ask.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "The more big dog ran fast." Right: "The bigger dog ran fast." Another weak sentence: "The boy went." Better: "The tired boy trudged home."
Step 6, Build a richer sentence from a simple one. Simple: "The bird sang." Richer: "The tiny red bird sang sweetly in the old tree." Underline verbs and adjectives to check you used both.
Step 7, Your turn. Make "The girl ran" richer with two adjectives and one stronger verb. Model answer: "The brave little girl raced down the dusty road."
Step 1, Notice the rhyme. Poem lines (my own): "The cat sat down on the warm red mat, / and watched a small bird, plump and fat." Rhyming words: mat and fat. Reason: the end sounds match.
Step 2, Read the poem with rhythm. Clap the beats: "The CAT sat DOWN on the WARM red MAT." Reason: reading with a steady beat shows the rhythm of the poem.
Step 3, Recite from memory by learning one line at a time. Say line one three times, add line two, then say both. Use gestures. Reason: small steps and actions help the memory.
Step 4, Find rhyming words for your poem. Pick "sun": run, fun, bun. Pick "light": night, bright, kite. Check that the end sounds match, even if the spelling differs ("blue" and "too").
Step 5, Write two lines. "I see a bright and shining star, / It twinkles from so far." Check: "star" and "far" rhyme, and the lines have a similar length.
Step 6, Fix an error. Wrong: "I like my dog, / he likes to play on the log, / and then he sleeps all day." The last line is long and has no rhyme. Right: "and then he curls up like a frog."
Step 7, Your turn. Finish this couplet with a rhyming word and explain the rhyme. "I put on my boot / and ran to the..." Model answer: "fruit" (boot and fruit rhyme: both end with the "oot" sound).

Step 1, Retell a short story in order. Story: "Dina lost her ball. She asked her friend. Her friend found it under the bench." Retell: "First Dina lost her ball. Then she asked her friend. At last it was found under the bench."
Step 2, Ask questions using who, what, where, why. "Who found the ball?" "Where did the friend find it?" "Why did Dina ask her friend?" Reason: question words show what kind of answer you need.
Step 3, Give a polite response. "Thank you for telling me." "That is a good idea." "I did not know that." Reason: a polite reply shows you listened.
Step 4, Listen then speak. Speaker: "I went to the market and bought a mango." Listener: "What colour was the mango?" Reason: a related question shows you were listening.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong response: "That is boring." Better: "I like the part about the market. Can you tell me more?" Another error: interrupting. Correction: wait until the speaker finishes, then speak.
Step 6, Use a complete sentence and a polite voice. "Please can I ask a question?" "Yes, go ahead." Reason: "please" and "thank you" make a conversation friendly.

Step 7, Your turn. Listen to: "I have a rabbit called Snow. It eats carrots." Ask one question and make one polite reply. Model answer: "What colour is Snow?" "That is a lovely name, thank you for telling me."
Step 1, Read the story in order. Short text (my own): "Mina found a tiny boat on the shore. She pushed it into the stream. It sailed away, and she waved goodbye." Notice the three actions in order.
Step 2, State the main idea in one sentence. "Mina sends a small boat down a stream." Reason: the main idea is what the whole text is about, not every detail.
Step 3, Pick the favourite part and give a reason. "My favourite part is when the boat sails away because I like to imagine where it goes." Reason: always use "because" after your choice.
Step 4, Use evidence from the text. Question: "How did Mina feel?" Answer: "She felt happy because she waved goodbye." Reason: a clue from the text supports your answer.
Step 5, Fix an error. Weak main idea: "A boat." Better: "A girl sends a boat down a stream." Another error: "I like it because it is good." Better: "I like it because the boat sails far."
Step 6, Read a poem aloud. Lines (my own): "Rain on the roof, tap-tap-tap, / Cat on the mat, nap-nap-nap." Notice repeated sounds and rhyme: tap and nap. Reason: sound patterns make a poem fun.

Step 7, Your turn. Read: "A fox saw a grape on a high vine. He jumped and jumped but could not reach it." State the main idea and your favourite part. Model answer: "A fox tries to reach a grape. I like the jumping because it is funny."
Step 1, Find the subject. Sentence: "The small bird sings." Ask: "Who or what sings?" Answer: "The small bird." That is the subject, the person or thing the sentence is about.

Step 2, Find the predicate. The rest, "sings", says what the subject does. In "The small bird sings in the tree", the predicate is "sings in the tree". Reason: the predicate tells what the subject does or is.
Step 3, Split sentences with a line. "My brother / plays football." "The big red bus / stopped at the corner." Subject on the left, predicate on the right. Reason: every full sentence has both.
Step 4, Spot an incomplete sentence. "Running down the hill." This has no subject. Fix: "The boys were running down the hill." Reason: a sentence needs a subject and a predicate.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "The tall girl." Right: "The tall girl waved." Also check: "Waved to her friend." Right: "She waved to her friend."
Step 6, Practise with a longer sentence. "Our new teacher reads stories every Friday." Subject: "Our new teacher". Predicate: "reads stories every Friday." Check each part by asking who and what.
Step 7, Your turn. Divide this: "The cold wind blew through the window." Model answer: subject: "The cold wind"; predicate: "blew through the window."
Step 1, Choose a pronoun to replace a noun. "Sara has a bag. She carries it to school." "Sara" becomes "she" and "bag" becomes "it". Reason: pronouns avoid repeating nouns.
Step 2, Use the right pronoun form. I/me, he/him, she/her, we/us, they/them. Model: "Rafi and I went home." "The teacher gave him a book." Subject: I. Object: me. Test by removing the other name.
Step 3, Choose an adjective for more detail. Instead of "a dog", write "a friendly, brown dog". Nouns: dog. Adjectives: friendly, brown. Reason: adjectives tell what kind or which one.

Step 4, Vary your sentences. Weak: "The cat is big. The cat is soft. The cat is white." Better: "The cat is big, soft and white." Or: "It is a big, soft, white cat." Reason: variety keeps the reader interested.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Me and him went to the park." Right: "He and I went to the park." Another error: "Their going home." Right: "They're going home." (They are.)

Step 6, Rewrite a paragraph with pronouns. Before: "Ali likes cricket. Ali plays cricket on Monday." After: "Ali likes cricket. He plays it on Monday." Reason: he replaces Ali and it replaces cricket.
Step 7, Your turn. Rewrite using pronouns and one adjective: "Mum made a cake. Mum put the cake on the table." Model answer: "Mum made a delicious cake. She put it on the table."
Step 1, Use the present for what is true now. "She walks to school." "The sun rises in the east." Add -s for he, she, it. Reason: the present simple names habits and facts.
Step 2, Use the past for what has finished. "She walked to school yesterday." Regular verbs end in -ed. Irregular: go, went; see, saw; make, made. Reason: the past tells what already happened.
Step 3, Use will for the future. "She will walk to school tomorrow." Or "going to": "She is going to walk." Reason: the future talks about things that have not happened yet.

Step 4, Keep tenses together. Right: "Yesterday we went to the market and bought mangoes." Wrong: "Yesterday we went to the market and buy mangoes." Reason: all actions in the same time need the same tense.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "He runned fast." Right: "He ran fast." Another error: "She will goes tomorrow." Right: "She will go tomorrow." After will, the verb stays plain.
Step 6, Change one sentence through three tenses. Present: "I paint a picture." Past: "I painted a picture." Future: "I will paint a picture." Mark the time word: now, yesterday, tomorrow.
Step 7, Your turn. Write "The children play cricket" in past and future. Model answer: past: "The children played cricket." Future: "The children will play cricket."

Step 1, Notice rhyme in a limerick (my own): "A baker named Dee made a pie, / It was tall and it touched the sky; / The cat took a bite, / And flew off in fright, / And the baker just waved goodbye." Rhyme scheme: A A B B A.
Step 2, Find the rhythm. Lines one, two and five are longer, with about three beats; lines three and four are shorter, with two beats. Clap: "A BAK-er named DEE made a PIE." Reason: limericks bounce.

Step 3, Pick the nonsense. The sky is touched by a pie and a cat flies off. Nonsense verse uses silly ideas, invented words and surprising events. Reason: the humour comes from impossible events told seriously.

Step 4, Plan your limerick. Choose a name and a rhyme: "Jack" rhymes with "back", "sack", "snack". Idea: Jack carries a snack. Write line one: "A boy who was called Jack..." Reason: the first line sets the rhyme.
Step 5, Write all five lines. "A boy who was called Jack / Packed a snack in his sack; / A bee came to stay, / And ate it all day, / So he went home with nothing in his pack." Check rhyme A A B B A.

Step 6, Fix an error. Wrong: "A boy who was called Jack / Took a snack in his park." Park does not rhyme with Jack. Right: "Took a snack in his sack." Choose words that really rhyme, not words only close in sound.
Step 7, Your turn. Write a limerick opening line and the rhyming second line about a goat named Moe. Model answer: "A goat who was named Moe / Wore a hat from head to toe," (Moe and toe rhyme).

Step 1, Plan a one-minute talk with three parts. Topic: "My pet fish". Beginning: "I'd like to tell you about my fish." Middle: two facts. End: "Thank you for listening." Reason: three parts keep the talk clear.
Step 2, Write key words, not the full text. Cue card: "fish - Bubbles - orange - eats flakes - swims round." Reason: key words keep your eyes up and your voice natural.

Step 3, Speak at a steady pace. Model opening: "Good morning, everyone. I'd like to tell you about my fish, Bubbles." Count about 130 words per minute for a one-minute talk. Reason: a steady pace helps people follow.
Step 4, Add one interesting detail. "Bubbles is orange, and she always swims to the top when she hears my voice." Reason: a personal detail makes your talk memorable.
Step 5, Ask a question about a talk. "Why did you choose the name Bubbles?" "How often do you feed her?" Reason: a question must be about what the speaker said.
Step 6, Fix an error. Wrong: speaking too fast and not looking up. Right: slow down and pause after each idea. Another weak question: "Is that all?" Better: "What does your fish eat?"
Step 7, Your turn. Prepare a 4-line cue card on "My favourite game" and one question to ask. Model answer: "game: football; friends; weekends; goal." Question: "How many players are on a team?"

Step 1, Start with a base word and a prefix. un- means not: happy becomes unhappy. re- means again: write becomes rewrite. dis- means not or opposite: agree becomes disagree. Reason: a prefix goes at the front and changes the meaning.

Step 2, Build with suffixes. -ful means full of: care becomes careful. -less means without: care becomes careless. -ly turns an adjective into an adverb: slow becomes slowly. Reason: a suffix goes at the end.
Step 3, Work out meanings by parts. "Unforgettable" = un- (not) + forget + -able (can be). Meaning: not able to be forgotten. Reason: splitting a word into parts reveals its meaning.

Step 4, Apply spelling rules. Drop silent e before -ing and -able: "hope" becomes "hoping". Change y to i before a suffix: "happy" becomes "happiness". Double the consonant in "run" before -ing: "running".
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "unhapyness". Right: "unhappiness" (un + happy, y to i, + ness). Another error: "carefull". Right: "careful" (the suffix is -ful with one l).

Step 6, Use new words in context. "The boy was careless and left his bag. His teacher was disappointed. He promised to recheck his work." Underline the prefix or suffix in each: careless, disappointed, recheck.

Step 7, Your turn. Build and define three words using un-, re- and -ful. Model answer: "unlock" (not locked); "retell" (tell again); "helpful" (full of help). Use one in a sentence: "She was helpful."
Step 1, Use adverbs to say how, when or where. "She spoke quietly." (how) "We left yesterday." (when) "He looked everywhere." (where) Reason: adverbs describe verbs.

Step 2, Change an adjective into an adverb with -ly. quick becomes quickly; careful becomes carefully; happy becomes happily. Irregular: good becomes well; fast stays fast. Model: "She runs fast and writes well."

Step 3, Use prepositions for position. "The cat is on the table." "The book is under the chair." "We walked across the bridge." Common ones: in, on, under, behind, between, through, across. Reason: they link a noun to the rest of the sentence.
Step 4, Add detail to a plain sentence. Plain: "The dog ran." Better: "The dog ran quickly across the yard and under the fence." Added adverb: quickly. Added prepositions: across, under.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "He plays good." Right: "He plays well." Another error: "She sat in front the door." Right: "She sat in front of the door." Remember: of follows "in front".

Step 6, Check position of adverbs. "Slowly, he opened the door." "He slowly opened the door." "He opened the door slowly." All work. Reason: adverbs of manner can move, but not between a verb and its object: not "He opened slowly the door".
Step 7, Your turn. Add one adverb and two prepositions: "The boy walked." Model answer: "The boy walked slowly along the path and through the gate."
Step 1, Prepare a short presentation with an opening, two reasons and a close. Topic: "We should plant more trees." Opening: "Today I will explain why our school needs more trees."

Step 2, Give a reason with evidence. "First, trees give shade. On hot days, students can play outside because the playground is cooler." Reason: a reason plus an example is stronger than a claim alone.
Step 3, Add a second reason. "Second, trees clean the air, so everyone breathes easier." Link ideas with first, second and finally. Reason: signpost words help the audience follow.

Step 4, Listen and respond with a reason. Classmate: "Trees drop leaves and make a mess." You: "I understand your point, but we can collect leaves for compost, so the mess becomes useful." Reason: respond to the point, then add your reason.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak response: "No, you are wrong." Better: "I see it differently because shade protects students from the sun." Another error: reading the text word by word. Right: use key words and look at the audience.
Step 6, Close and invite questions. "To sum up, trees give shade and clean air, so we should plant more. Thank you. Are there any questions?" Reason: the summary repeats the main message.

Step 7, Your turn. Write one reason with because and one respectful response to a different view about the school library. Model answer: "We need a bigger library because many students share a few books." Response: "I see your point about cost, but books last for years."

Step 1, Join two sentences with a coordinating conjunction. Two sentences: "I like tea. I don't like coffee." Joined: "I like tea, but I don't like coffee." Use FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so, with a comma before it.

Step 2, Join with a subordinating conjunction. "I took an umbrella because it was raining." "Although it was late, we kept working." Reason: a subordinate clause cannot stand alone; the main clause can.
Step 3, Use a comma after an introductory clause. "When the bell rang, the students left." "If you study, you will pass." Reason: the comma separates the introductory clause from the main clause.
Step 4, Use pronouns to avoid repeating. Repeated: "Rina took Rina's book and gave Rina's book to Rina's friend." Better: "Rina took her book and gave it to her friend." Pronouns: her, it.

Step 5, Fix an error. Run-on: "I was tired I went to bed." Right: "I was tired, so I went to bed." Fragment: "Because it was raining." Right: "We stayed home because it was raining." A clause beginning with because needs a main clause.

Step 6, Check the pronoun reference. Unclear: "Ali told Sam that he was late." Who is "he"? Clear: "Ali told Sam, 'You are late.'" or "Ali told Sam that Ali was late." Reason: every pronoun must have one clear noun.

Step 7, Your turn. Join and shorten: "Maya was hungry. Maya made a sandwich. The sandwich was big." Model answer: "Because Maya was hungry, she made a big sandwich." Or: "Maya was hungry, so she made a big sandwich."
Step 1, Use a prefix to unlock a meaning. "Pre-" means before: preview is a view before. "Inter-" means between: international is between nations. "Sub-" means under: submarine is under the sea.

Step 2, Use a root to unlock families. Root "port" means carry: transport (carry across), export (carry out), portable (can be carried). Reason: one root makes many words, and knowing it helps you guess unfamiliar words.

Step 3, Use a suffix to find word class. -tion makes a noun: educate becomes education. -able makes an adjective: read becomes readable. -ly makes an adverb: clear becomes clearly. Reason: the ending signals what the word does.
Step 4, Trace an origin. The word "telephone" joins Greek tele (far) and phone (sound): a far sound. Also "telescope" (far + see). Reason: shared roots link words and give clues to meaning.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "The submarine is above the water" (a student thinking sub- means up). Right: "The submarine travels below the water." Check the prefix meaning against the context.

Step 6, Work out an unknown word. Sentence: "The scientist wanted to transport the samples across the country." Clue: trans- (across) + port (carry). Meaning: to carry across. Check: it fits the sentence.

Step 7, Your turn. Define "unpredictable" and "export" using parts. Model answer: "unpredictable" = un- (not) + pre- (before) + dict (say) + -able (can be): cannot be said beforehand. "Export" = ex- (out) + port (carry): to carry out.
Step 1, State your opinion in one sentence. "I believe schools should start later in the morning." Reason: a clear opinion tells the audience what you are arguing.

Step 2, Support with reasons and evidence. "First, teenagers need more sleep; studies show tired students learn less. Second, later starts reduce late arrivals." Reason: each reason needs support so it is not just opinion.
Step 3, Respond to a different view. Opponent: "A later start means a later finish." You: "That's true, but afternoon clubs can adjust their schedules." Reason: acknowledge the point, then answer it.
Step 4, Use debate phrases. "I agree that..., but..." "That is a fair point; however..." "On the other hand..." Reason: these phrases keep a debate respectful and organised.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "You are wrong because it is just stupid." Better: "I disagree because evidence shows the opposite." Another error: attacking the person. Right: challenge the idea, not the speaker.
Step 6, Close the argument. "In conclusion, a later start improves sleep, learning and punctuality, so I urge the school to change." Reason: a conclusion repeats your opinion and ends strongly.

Step 7, Your turn. Give an opinion on homework with two reasons and a reply to a different view. Model answer: "Homework should be short because rest matters, and because family time matters. Some say it builds discipline; however, short tasks can do that too."

Step 1, Choose the right pronoun. Subject: I, he, she, we, they. Object: me, him, her, us, them. Model: "She gave him the book." "Between you and me, it was easy." Reason: use object forms after verbs and prepositions.

Step 2, Match the tense to the time. Present: "She studies every night." Past: "She studied last night." Present perfect: "She has studied for an hour." Future: "She will study tomorrow." Reason: the time word guides the tense.

Step 3, Use the four sentence types. Statement: "The library opens at nine." Question: "When does it open?" Command: "Please close the door." Exclamation: "What a lovely surprise!" Reason: each type has a purpose and punctuation.
Step 4, Check subject-verb agreement. "The team plays well." "The boys play well." "Neither of the answers is correct." Reason: the verb agrees with the subject, not the nearest noun.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Me and her goes to the market." Right: "She and I go to the market." Another error: "He have finished his work." Right: "He has finished his work."

Step 6, Rewrite a paragraph with consistent tense. Before: "Yesterday, I walk to school and see my friend." After: "Yesterday, I walked to school and saw my friend." Underline the verbs to check them.

Step 7, Your turn. Write one sentence of each type about a school trip. Model answer: "We visited the museum." "What did you see there?" "Please bring your notebook." "How amazing the dinosaurs were!"
Step 1, Plan the talk in minutes. Topic: "A book I recommend". Opening: 30 seconds. Main points: two minutes. Close: 30 seconds. Reason: planning time keeps you from rushing or running out.

Step 2, Write an opening that catches attention. "Have you ever read a story that you could not put down? Today I want to tell you about one." Reason: a question or a surprising fact draws the audience in.
Step 3, Use short cue cards. Card: "Title; main character; one exciting moment; why I recommend it." Reason: cards hold prompts, not the full script, so your voice stays natural.

Step 4, Give feedback with a model. Use: two stars and a wish. "Your voice was clear and the examples were interesting. Next time, slow down a little." Reason: praise first, then one specific suggestion, is useful and kind.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak feedback: "It was fine." Better: "I liked how you described the main character. Your ending was clear." Another error: criticising the speaker. Right: describe what you saw or heard.

Step 6, Close the talk and invite a reply. "To sum up, this story is exciting and thoughtful, so I recommend it. Thank you. Any questions?" Reason: ending with a summary and thanks tells the audience you are done.

Step 7, Your turn. Write the opening line and a two stars and a wish feedback for a classmate's talk on football. Model answer: "Opening: What makes a team win? Feedback: Clear voice, good facts. Next time, look at the audience more."

Step 1, Prepare for a discussion by listing three points on the topic. Topic: "Should schools ban phones?" Points: distraction, safety, learning tools. Reason: you can join in confidently when you have notes ready.
Step 2, Start the discussion. "I'd like to begin by saying that phones are useful in emergencies, but they can also distract students." Reason: a short opening position invites replies.

Step 3, Use turn-taking phrases. Agree: "I agree with Sara because..." Disagree: "I see it differently because..." Add: "Building on that, ..." Interrupt politely: "Can I add something here?" Reason: these phrases keep discussion respectful.
Step 4, Support a point with evidence. "In my class, students check phones during lessons and miss instructions." Reason: a real example makes a point credible.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "That is wrong." Better: "I'm not sure I agree, because many students use phones for research." Another error: speaking for five minutes. Right: keep each turn to about thirty seconds.

Step 6, Prepare one minute without notes. Structure: "Point, reason, example, close." Model: "Phones should be limited. They distract learners. For example, I missed a quiz question yesterday. So a limit helps."

Step 7, Your turn. Give a one-minute point on "School uniforms" with point, reason, example and close. Model answer: "Uniforms help students. They reduce pressure about clothes. In my school, nobody compares brands. So uniforms keep it fair."
Step 1, Plan slides around one message. Topic: "Reducing plastic at school". Slide 1: title. Slide 2: the problem. Slide 3: two solutions. Slide 4: next steps. Reason: one slide, one idea.
Step 2, Write slide text in short phrases. Slide 3: "Reusable bottles; refill stations." Do not copy full paragraphs. Reason: the audience listens to you and reads only keywords.

Step 3, Use a script for spoken text. Say: "Every day, our canteen throws away about 200 plastic bottles. That is the weight of a small car after one month." Reason: speaking adds information that the slide does not show.
Step 4, Choose a clear visual. A bar chart comparing bottles used: Monday 210, Tuesday 190, Wednesday 205. Label axes. Reason: a labelled chart is easier to interpret than a list of numbers.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: reading the slide aloud word for word and facing the screen. Right: look at the audience, and say the key point in your own words. Another error: seven bullets on one slide. Right: two or three.
Step 6, Rehearse transitions. "Now that we have seen the problem, let's look at two solutions." "To conclude, small changes add up." Reason: transitions make the talk flow from slide to slide.

Step 7, Your turn. Plan a four-slide presentation on "Healthy lunch". Model answer: slide 1 title, slide 2 "Why lunch matters", slide 3 "Three healthy ideas: fruit, rice and beans, water", slide 4 "Make one change tomorrow".
Step 1, State a claim clearly. "Schools should teach financial literacy." Reason: a precise claim lets the audience judge your reasoning.

Step 2, Build the argument with PEEL. Point: "Financial skills prepare students for adult life." Evidence: "Many young adults borrow without understanding interest." Explain: "Understanding interest prevents debt." Link: "So schools should teach it."

Step 3, Anticipate a counter-argument. "Some say the curriculum is already full. However, a short weekly lesson can replace less useful content." Reason: addressing the other side makes your argument credible.

Step 4, Respond to a challenge with reasons. Challenger: "Parents should teach this." You: "I agree that parents help, but not every family can. School ensures equal access." Reason: acknowledge, then argue.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "Everyone knows money is important." Better: "Surveys show many students struggle with budgeting." Another error: overgeneralising ("always", "never"). Right: "often", "many", "in most cases".

Step 6, Use rhetorical techniques sparingly. Rule of three: "clear, practical and fair." Rhetorical question: "How can we expect adults to budget if no one ever taught them?" Reason: they add emphasis, but too many sound forced.

Step 7, Your turn. Write a PEEL paragraph for "Students should have a say in school rules". Model answer: "Students should help set rules. Students follow rules they understand. Therefore, school councils improve behaviour, so schools should involve them."

Step 1, Analyse the prompt. Prompt: "Describe a technology that has changed daily life, and explain whether the change is positive." Key words: describe, explain, whether positive. Reason: you must do all three tasks.
Step 2, Plan with a quick frame. Introduction: name the technology. Body: two effects with examples. Judgement: positive or mixed. Close: summary. Reason: a frame stops you from rambling.

Step 3, Start with a strong opening. "One technology that has changed daily life is the smartphone; it connects us to information, people and services in seconds." Reason: a direct opening answers the prompt immediately.

Step 4, Develop with examples and reasons. "It saves time; for example, I can pay bills without going to the bank. However, it can also reduce face-to-face conversation." Reason: balance shows critical thinking.

Step 5, Respond to a follow-up question. Examiner: "Do you think people rely on phones too much?" You: "In many cases, yes. For instance, people use maps rather than learn routes, though this saves time." Reason: give a position, an example and a limit.

Step 6, Fix an error. Weak: "Phones are good. They are good because they are good." Better: "Phones are useful because they give instant access to information." Another error: very short answers. Extend with a reason or example.

Step 7, Your turn. Answer in two sentences: "Is online learning as effective as classroom learning?" Model answer: "It can be effective for self-disciplined students because it is flexible. However, classrooms offer discussion and support, so I think a mix is best."
